claims.text: Economic development brings benefits such as jobs, wages, roads and services, but its activities may also pose threats to the natural environment and to people, and the threats work at two scales: local threats, such as a river polluted below a works or a hillside eroded by overgrazing, harm one area, while global threats, above all enhanced global warming, affect the whole planet because greenhouse gases released anywhere mix through the whole atmosphere.

claims.text: Overcultivation, overgrazing and the felling of trees expose bare soil to wind and rain, which causes soil erosion - the loss of the fertile topsoil that plants need. In dry districts, if the loss of vegetation and topsoil continues, the land can undergo desertification, the spread of desert-like conditions into land that previously supported crops or herds, which thins harvests and pushes herding families towards towns.

claims.text: Burning fossil fuels in power stations, factories and vehicles releases carbon dioxide, and cattle, rice growing and rotting waste add methane; these greenhouse gases trap some of the heat radiated from the Earth's surface, and the extra gas from human activity traps more, warming the atmosphere further - the enhanced greenhouse effect, usually called enhanced global warming. This is separate from the thinning of the ozone layer, which lets more ultraviolet light through: greenhouse gases trap heat, while a thinner ozone layer lets ultraviolet in, and the two problems are not the same.

claims.text: Pollution is the release into the environment of a substance or a form of energy that harms the environment or the people in it. The four kinds named in the syllabus are water pollution (sewage, industrial waste and farm run-off in rivers, lakes and the sea), air pollution (smoke and gases such as sulphur dioxide from burning fuel and smelting metal), noise pollution (traffic, machinery, aircraft and building works) and visual pollution (derelict works, scrap heaps, pylons and litter). A threat should be named precisely - a gas such as sulphur dioxide, a water pollutant such as raw sewage, a process such as soil erosion by wind and rain - because vague words such as "pollution" or "the environment is damaged" leave a reader unable to identify the pollutant or the process.

claims.text: Sustainable development is development that meets present needs without reducing the ability of future generations to meet theirs.

verification.method: Authored originally for the 0460 learner resource under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: The threats that can accompany development are the reason sustainable development and management are needed: growth that pollutes, erodes and exhausts leaves less for the people who come after. Sustainable management therefore sets limits on what is taken and released, conserves the resource the activity depends on, and keeps the benefits local - treating waste before it is released, replanting what is felled, capping visitor numbers - so that the economy can keep working beyond one generation.

verification.method: Authored originally for the 0460 learner resource under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: Sustainable development does not mean building more of everything: a plan that builds without limit can exhaust the very resource it depends on. The test of a sustainable plan is whether the resource will still be there for the next generation - a reef under a capped number of divers, a forest felled no faster than it regrows - which is a different test from how much a project builds.

verification.method: Authored originally for the 0460 learner resource under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: Resource conservation means using resources carefully so that they last, keeping the supply for future users. Renewable resources such as fish stocks, forests, water and soil can replace what is taken provided they are harvested no faster than they renew, so conserving them means quotas, replanting and rotation; non-renewable resources such as minerals and fossil fuels cannot be replaced within a human lifetime, so conserving them means using them more slowly and more efficiently, reusing and recycling what has already been won from the ground.

verification.method: Authored originally for the 0460 learner resource under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: Conservation matters because overuse can destroy a resource together with the livelihoods resting on it: an overfished lake can take decades to recover, cleared woodland exposes soil to erosion, and wasted water shortens a town's supply. Conserving resources also means less mining, felling, manufacturing and dumping, which reduces pollution and the emissions that drive enhanced global warming, so conserved resources keep serving the next generation.

claims.text: Kabwe is a mining town in central Zambia, about 140 kilometres north of the capital, Lusaka, on the main north-south railway; lead and zinc were mined and smelted there from about 1906 until the mine closed in 1994. The workings and waste dumps lie in the middle of the town, with townships such as Kasanda and Chowa beside them, and the town is still growing, with homes spreading onto ground the mine left contaminated.

verification.method: Authored originally for the 0460 learner resource under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: Kabwe's risk was built in two ways: nearly ninety years of smelting released lead-rich smoke that settled into the township soil, and the waste dumps left behind blow lead-bearing dust over the town in the dry season, so children swallow lead with the soil and dust on their hands and food. Lead is a poison that harms the developing brain and nervous system, and studies in the 2000s and 2010s found soil-lead values many times above guideline levels and some of the highest blood-lead levels recorded in children anywhere.

verification.method: Authored originally for the 0460 learner resource under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: The response at Kabwe shows management catching up with a legacy: a clean-up backed with international funding, begun in the late 2010s, has been capping the worst dumps with clean soil and treating the ground around homes and schools, while health teams test children's blood. The task is slow because the pollution sits in the soil itself rather than in one pipe that can be closed, which is the sharpest lesson of the case: risks prevented while development is still taking place cost far less to manage than risks left to settle into the ground.
